Keywords: antiglutamic acid
decarboxylase antibodies, continuous
motor unit activity, epidural anesthesia,
focal stiﬀ person syndrome, stiﬀ leg
syndrome, stiﬀ limb syndrome
doi:10.1111/ene.12923
Received: 21 May 2015
Accepted: 4 November 2015
Dear Sir,
Stiﬀ leg syndrome (SLS) is an uncom-
mon focal variant of the stiﬀ person syn-
drome and is characterized by stiﬀness
and painful spasms of the lower limbs,
with no axial involvement. Typical elec-
trophysiological ﬁndings include continu-
ous motor unit activity (CMUA) at rest
and abnormally increased exteroceptive
reﬂexes [1,2]. The results of antiglutamic
acid decarboxylase (anti-GAD) antibody
testing are usually negative [3]. We report
on two patients who developed SLS after
epidural anesthesia.

cases.text:
Patient 1
A 78-year-old woman with Lewy body
dementia and very mild parkinsonian
signs was admitted to Hospital General
Universitario Gregorio Mara ~n/C19on
(Madrid, Spain) for replacement of a
right hip prosthesis. She was not taking
antiparkinsonian treatment. Surgery was
performed under epidural anesthesia with
bupivacaine and fentanyl. Within 7 days
after surgery, the patient complained of a
progressive abnormal ﬁxed posture of the
right foot with forced inversion and plan-
tar ﬂexion. A few days later, this posture
became bilateral, with stiﬀness and pain
in both feet that impaired walking. The
remainder of the neurological examina-
tion revealed cognitive impairment and
very mild akinesia in the upper limbs.
No spasms were observed.

Patient 2
An 83-year-old woman with Parkinson’s
disease and moderate akynetic-rigid syn-
drome with no motor ﬂuctuations or
dyskinesias had surgery under epidural
anesthesia with bupivacaine and fentanyl
for a fracture of the left hip. In the imme-
diate postoperative period the patient
developed an irreducible, stiﬀ and painful
posture in ﬂexion, external rotation of the
right hip, and forced ﬂexion of the knee
with no spasms. The remainder of the
neurological examination was unremark-
able apart from very mild parkinsonian
signs in the other extremities. Her usual
antiparkinsonian medication (levodopa
950 mg/day) was unchanged.
In both cases the neurophysiological
study showed CMUA (Fig. 1a) at rest in
antagonist muscles of the aﬀected limbs
and enhanced exteroceptive reﬂexes
(Fig. 1b) with distal and bilateral diﬀu-
sion and late grouped electromyographic
responses (patient 1). Central motor

conduction to the lower limbs was nor-
mal. Serum anti-GAD antibody testing
was negative in both cases. Spinal mag-
netic resonance imaging showed lumbar
stenosis and mild signs of arachnoiditis
in patient 1 and was normal in patient 2.
Brain magnetic resonance imaging was
normal in both cases. Treatment with
oral baclofen and injections of botulinum
toxin was ineﬀective (case 1) and a
partial improvement was observed with
clonazepam (case 2). The clinical picture
remained unchanged after a follow-up of
2.2 years (patient 1) and 2 months (pa-
tient 2). Both patients were wheelchair-
bound.
We describe two cases in which the clin-
ical and electrophysiological ﬁndings were
consistent with SLS after the application
of epidural anesthesia. To our knowledge,
this is the ﬁrst report of such an associa-
tion. Both patients underwent unilateral
hip surgery, but the stiﬀness involved
both lower limbs or the contralateral leg.
The neurophysiological ﬁndings suggest
an impairment of spinal inhibitory
interneurons. We hypothesized that this
could be related to a local inﬂammatory
process triggered by the epidural anesthe-
sia or even to a direct neurotoxic eﬀect of
bupivacaine and fentanyl [4]. It is note-
worthy that both patients had synucle-
inopathies and it is known that in patients
with Parkinson’s disease a-synuclein
inclusions were found in the spinal cord,
although their role as a possible predis-
posing factor remains unclear.

References

form of stiﬀ-man syndrome. Ann Neurol

3. Barker RA, Revestz T, Thom M, Mars-
den CD, Brown P. Review of 23 patients
aﬀected by the stiﬀ man syndrome: clini-
cal subdivision into stiﬀ trunk (man)
syndrome, stiﬀ limb syndrome, and pro-
gressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity. J
Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 1998; 65:
633–640.
4. Abut YC, Turkmen AZ, Midi A, Eren B,
Yener N, Nurten A. Neurotoxic eﬀects
